note: Finds most oncology AI never prospectively validated and equity considerations largely missing, which are two standing audit findings.
title: Prospective evaluation of artificial intelligence (AI) applications for use in cancer pathways following diagnosis: a systematic review

reading.body:
Only 15 prospective evaluations of post-diagnosis oncology AI appeared across a decade of searching, and most of that work stayed experimental.

The pattern is a gap between activity and evidence. The review searched from January 2013 through May 2023 and found 15 forward looking studies. Most oncology AI projects never reached prospective validation in clinical settings, and few connected measured performance to better patient outcomes. Fairness and practical factors like time, cost, and resources were largely absent.

For AI in cancer care, the binding constraint is not model capability but proof in real clinical settings. A tool that performs well in development but is never prospectively tested cannot be adopted, and one that ignores fairness or system compatibility cannot be deployed at scale. The review's own recommendations point to collaborative implementation studies aligned with local health systems, which is an argument about evidence and integration rather than about compute.

What this does not cover: the data gives no counts by cancer type, no breakdown of which AI methods were used, and no measure of how many projects exist outside the 15 that were prospectively evaluated. It also says nothing about the compute, buildings, or power behind these tools, so no claim about infrastructure can be drawn from it. The 43 citations indicate the review is being read, not that its findings have changed.

explain_beginner: This review looked at studies where artificial intelligence was used in cancer care after a diagnosis, not just for finding cancer. The authors searched medical databases and found only 15 studies that tested these tools in real, forward looking ways between 2013 and 2023. Most artificial intelligence projects stayed experimental. They were not properly checked in clinical practice, and many did not show clear patient benefit. The review also found little attention to fairness or to practical issues like time, cost, and resources. This matters because hospitals need proof that these tools work, help patients, and treat people fairly before adopting them widely.
explain_business: This review suggests that most artificial intelligence tools for cancer care after diagnosis are not yet ready for routine adoption. The authors found only 15 forward looking evaluations, and most projects stayed experimental, lacked proof of patient benefit, and did not address fairness or practical demands like time, cost, and resources. For executives, this means claims about artificial intelligence improving cancer pathways should be treated cautiously. Investment and procurement decisions should require evidence from real clinical settings, clear outcome measures, and plans for fairness and system compatibility. It also points toward funding collaborative implementation studies with local health systems rather than buying unproven tools.
explain_practitioner: The authors systematically reviewed artificial intelligence used in cancer care after diagnosis. They searched PubMed and Web of Science for articles from January 2013 through May 2023 and found 15 prospective evaluations. They assessed study quality with standard appraisal tools for trials and nonrandomized intervention studies, and they examined time, cost, and resource factors. Most oncology artificial intelligence work remained experimental. Few studies showed validity in clinical settings or connected measured performance to better patient outcomes. Research was also limited by inconsistent methods and poor compatibility between health systems. Implementation and fairness were rarely assessed. The authors recommend collaborative implementation studies aligned with current standards and local systems.
